Documents related to an Agenda item are available to the public in the City Clerk’s Office located at
320 West Newmark Avenue, Monterey Park, CA 91754, during normal business hours and the City’s

PUBLIC COMMENTS ON AGENDA ITEMS
You may speak up to 5 minutes on Agenda item. You may combine up to 2 minutes of time with
another person’s speaking. No person may speak more than a total of 10 minutes. The Mayor and City
Council may change the amount of time allowed for speakers.
Per the Americans with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in this meeting
please call City Hall at (626) 307-1359 for reasonable accommodation at least 24 hours before a

This Agenda includes items considered by the City Council acting on behalf of the Successor Agency

It is recommended that the City Council:

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The Movember Foundation is the leading global organization committed to changing the
face of men's health. The Movember community has raised $800 million to date and
funded over 1,200 programs in 21 countries. This work is saving and improving the lives
of men affected by prostate cancer, testicular cancer and mental health problems.

The Foundation challenges men to grow moustaches during Movember (formerly known
as November), to spark conversation and raise vitalfunds for its men's health programs.
To date, over 5 million moustaches have been grown worldwide.

The mustaches are a symbol to promote awareness regarding men's health issues and
to encourage yearly checkups regarding prostate and testicular cancer. The growth of a
new moustache prompts a conversation, which in turn generates awareness and
educates people on the health issues men face.

The Vision of the Movember Foundation is to have an everlasting impact on the face of
men's health.

RECOMMENDATION:

Pursuant to its direction on October 16,2019, it is recommended that the City Council
consider:

  1. Adopting a resolution adding a question to the ballot for the previously called
  general municipal election on March 3,2020 in accordance with Monterey Park
  Municipal Code ("MPMC') S 2.04.080 to elect members of the City Council from
  Council Districts 2,3, and 4;

  2. Alternatively, but not recommended, the City Council may consider
  a. Adopting an urgency ordinance repealing district-based elections and to
  reinstate at-large elections for the March 2020 general municipal election;

  b. Adding a proposition to the March 3, 2020 ballot which proposes district
  elections on a go fonryard basis after the March 3,2020 Ballot (primarily for the
  purpose of allowing the electorate to choose the election sequencing of future
  d istrict elections); and/or

  3. Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

"Preserying the integrity of the electoral process, preventing corruption, and sustaining
the active, alert responsibility of the individual citizen in a democracy for the wise conduct
of government are interests of the highest importance."l The current sitting City Council
engaged in a 1S-month process (including seven public hearings, several noticed
meetings, and numerous discussions) which concluded in May 2019 with the Council
deciding to switch from an at-large to a district- based Council Member election process
in compliance with the California Voting Rights Act ("CVRA"). This was intended to avoid
a likely successful and very expensive legal challenge to the City's at-large election
process. Switching back to an at-large election, even if it is just for one election cycle, just
days before the nomination period opens for candidates to begin qualifying to run for City
Council is extremely risky from a legal perspective and very likely indefensible. ln fact, it

1 (lnternal punctuation
  omitted) First Nat. Bank of Boston v. Bellotti(1978) 435 U.S. 765,788-789

  Page 10 of 214
 could result in a court imposing its own district-based process upon the City either before
or after the March 2020 election, and the potential invalidation of the March election
results if the Council switches back to an at-large process.

More specifically, as to ltem No. 2(a) above, it does not appear that findings can be made
to support adoption of an urgency ordinance. The City's administrative record developed
over 1S-months for transitioning from at-large to district elections clearly shows that
changing back to at-large elections would expose the City to significant liability under the
CVRA and Civil Rights law. lt does not appear that there is any legitimate basis to defend
against a potential challenge to such an urgency ordinance. lf it loses a legal challenge,
the City would pay not only for its own defense costs but also those of the prevailing party
Taking the action in ltem No. 2(a) is contrary to existing law and to the main reason that
the entire City Council commenced implementing (and the majority of the City Council
approved) the district election process.

The same legal issues also arise regarding ltem No. 2(b): if the City Council repealed
district elections pursuant to ltem No. 2(a), the City could be immediately sued by persons
asserting that such action constitutes CVRA and Civil Rights violations. This is true even
though on October 16th the Council majority discussed the potential thatthe Citywould
return to district-based elections in the future and give voters the chance to decide the
sequence of district elections. Because three City Council seats are up for election in
March 2020, the current Council cannot commit the next City Council to take such an
action. ln addition to the legal risks identified above (as explained below in detail), if the
City reverts back to at-large voting it must restart the process for switching back to district-
based voting (which requires at least four public hearings). There is insufficient time to
complete this process for the March 2020 election as the cutoff date for placing matters
on the ballot is December 6,2019. Finally, there are 10 different potential combinations
for sequencing the district elections. This would require 10 different ballot questions to
determine which option the electorate prefers (the ballot measure receiving the most
votes would prevail). A cost estimate for these 10 ballot propositions is approximately
$230,000 (County fees to place on ballot), plus staff and legal costs.

Accordingly, it is strongly recommended that the Council only take the action in ltem No.
1.

BACKGROUND:

Before reviewing the probable consequences of repealing district-based elections, it is
important to review why the City Council completed the transition from at-large to district
elections earlier this year. This is crucial for the context of this Staff Report and to
understand the administrative record that would be reviewed by a court if there is a legal
challenge filed against the City.

The effective date of the transition to district-based voting was May 31 ,2019. That is
when district-based elections became law. Those regulations are codified in the
Monterey Park Municipal Code ("MPMC") at $$ 2.04.060 to 2.04.090 (the "District

  Page 2 of 15

  Page 11 of 214
 Election"). Notably, there has been no change in the CVRA since the City's district-
based election system became the law. Accordingly, all the same significant legal
issues and financial exposure identified by the City Council beginning in February 2018
still exist.

The City Council began discussing the question of district elections in 2013. ln that year,
Council Member Real Sebastian identified district voting as a discussion item during
strategic plan meetings. Subsequently, the City Council considered the matter at its
meeting on December 18, 2013. At that time, the City Council discussed a staff report
which provided an overview of the process required to implement such a change
including determining "which districts are up for election first." Various considerations
were discussed for changing the City's election process. This included Council Member
Real Sebastian's stated reason that district elections would result in better
representation for constituents within the districts. Ultimately, however, the Council's
consensus was to postpone the matter for a future (but unspecified) meeting.

On February 7,2018, Council Member lng asked about district elections during a
Council meeting noting that he believed that "district voting is the law." Council Member
Real Sebastian placed the matter onto the March 7, 2018 City Council meeting for
discussion. As part of Council Member Real Sebastian's staff report, and during verbal
comments, Council Members Real Sebastian and lng urged the City Council to initiate
the process for changing to a district-based election process. Among other things, the
Council Members stated that multiple cities were being sued for utilizing at-large
election processes; that cities fighting such lawsuits were paying millions of dollars in
attorneys' fees; and that "at any moment" the City of Monterey Park would be served.
The City Attorney's office advised that if the City Council wanted to proceed with district
elections to avoid liability issues it should consider adopting an ordinance to implement
this type of election process since placing the matter on the ballot for voter
consideration would expose the City to risk and be confusing to the voters: if the voters
disapproved district elections, an interested party could still force districting upon the
City through a court action.

Based upon City Council direction on March 7th, the City contracted with National
Demographics Corporation ("NDC') on July 6,2018 to begin compiling data to draft
election district maps. Following a series of closed session meetings in 2018 regarding
the matter (as anticipated litigation), the City Council announced on October 3,2018
that an item would be placed on the October 17,2018 City Council agenda to discuss
whether the City should begin the process of transitioning from at-large to district
elections. That agenda item was continued from October 17th until the November 7  ,

2018 meeting to ensure all Council Members were present to discuss the matter.

On October 18,2018, the City received a letter from Mr. Kevin Shenkman on behalf of
his client, the Southwest Voter Registration Education Project (the "SVREP")
threatening legal action absent the City's voluntarily change to a district-based election

  Page 3 of 15

  Page 12 of 214
 process. By letter dated October 19,2018, the City Attorney's office informed Mr.
Shenkman that the City began the process well before receiving his letter and that he
was welcome to participate in the public input process.

On November7,2018, the City Council held extensive discussions regarding the
CVRA. During that meeting, the City Council asked numerous questions - and posed
several hypotheticals - to both the City Attorney and to NDC's representative, Mr.
Robert McEntire. Among other things, the City Council was informed about the
following:

  a  The way the CVRA is written, even if there has been adequate ethnic
  representation on a city council (commensurate with the ethnic populations in the
  City), a City will lose a lawsuit if it does not switch from at-large to district
  elections. This was very relevant to Monterey Park since during the past two
  decades the composition of the City Council was representative of the City's
  ethnic demographics;

  The CVRA is designed to allow minority groups to vote for a person of their
  choice which could be a person other than of their own ethnicity;

  a  lf the City Council chooses not to switch election methodology, there is an
  "extreme likelihood" that the City would lose a lawsuit, if one were filed, and have
  districts imposed upon it by court order;

  a  As a result of such a lawsuit, the City would be forced under the CVRA to pay
  millions of dollars in attorneys' fees to its own legal counsel and the plaintiff's
  attorney;

  a  lf the City were to place the question on the ballot, i.e., ask voters whether the
  City should switch election methods, it would still face lawsuits and have districts
  imposed by a court if voters chose an at-large method of elections. Additionally,
  this could be confusing to voters as they would be under the impression that their
  determination would represent the final decision on the issue;

  a  It would be impractical for the City Council to choose a map and then seek voter
  ratification for that map in 2020 since such a map would apply proactively, i.e., it
  would first apply only to the 2022 election, and the City will need to consider new
  maps in 2021 which is when the United States census data becomes available;

  a  The voluntary process for receiving public input regarding district elections would
  conclude with the City Council selecting an appropriate map, and the map must
  include "the election sequence"2;

2 Mr. McEntire at1 01'.22.

  Page 4 of 15

  Page 13 of 214
   a  Moving to a district-based election would not affect the City's term limit
  regulations; and

  a  lnitiating action without a threat of litigation would provide more time to
  implement district-based voting than to be forced to take action in 90 days based
  upon receiving a threat of legal action (as would be required by the CVRA).

Most Council Members disfavored changing from at-large to district-based voting:
Council Members Chan, lng, Lam, and Liang all spoke out against such a change for
various reasons. All Council Members, however, believed that voter input at an election
was desirable and were disappointed that the CVRA would not - as a practical matter  -
allow that to occur. Council Member Real Sebastian opined that moving to district
elections was fiscally prudent since the City had now received a threat of litigation from
SVREP and that Mr. Shenkman, SVREP's attorney, was likely to be watching the
meeting. Switching election systems might even have some hidden positives.

Ultimately, the City Council unanimously adopted the resolution commencing the
process for switching to district-based elections. The reasons expressed by all Council
Members for that decision was concern regarding the financial impact of not taking such
action.

On November 21,2018, the City Council again considered the CVRA in the context of
Mayor Peter Chan's recommendation that the City consider lobbying the California
Legislature to amend the CVRA. He asked for $25,000 to be allocated toward the effort

Council Member Real Sebastian noted that if the City did not comply with the CVRA,
then it would be faced with a lawsuit. Council Member lng noted that he agreed that
nothing required fixing - the at-large system was working He expressed concern,
however, that other cities such as South Pasadena paid out millions of dollars trying to
fight CVRA lawsuits. And, he noted that it was unlikely a lobbyist would change
anything. Ultimately, the City Council voted to continue the discussion to its December
5,2018 meeting.

On December 5, 2018, the City Council considered two items related to district-based
voting. First, it concluded its discussion regarding Council Member Chan's idea of
lobbying to change the CVRA itself. As to that item, the City Council (specifically
Council Member Real Sebastian) discussed the potential futility of seeking to change
the CVRA as multiple groups - including the ACLU, MALDEF, NAACP, NALEO, Asian
Americans Advancing Justice (AAAJ), and Lawyers' Committee for Civil Rights of the
San Francisco Bay Area - all supported the CVRA. Based upon that support, it was
unlikely that the California Legislature would make changes to the CVRA.

Also on December Sth was the first public hearing for the process of changing to a
district-based election system. Mr. McEntire provided an overview of the process.
Among other things, Mr. McEntire explained that the CVRA was written to ensure
attorneys got paid their fees from legal challenges. He further noted that it is quite

  Page 5 of 15

  Page 14 of 214
 obvious that the CVRA prefers district elections and that he frequently finds that the final
map selected by the City Council may be an amalgamation of several maps proposed
by community members. Discussion among the City Council centered on examples of
other cities that fought against demands that those jurisdictions change to district
elections. ln the end, those cities lost and paid millions of dollars to both their own
attorneys and the plaintiffs' attorneys.

The City Council held a second public hearing on December 19, 2018. Mr. McEntire
again provided an overview and reminded the City Council regarding the multiple
jurisdictions that fought CVRA claims and ended up settling or losing cases. Council
Member lng noted that there were over 100 cities that were sued and more than 170
school districts. He further cited to the City of Palmdale as an example of what could
happen in the extreme where the City settled a case for $4.7M and also expended more
than $2M in its own defense costs. During his presentation, Mr. McEntire repeated that
the final choice regarding district maps lay with the City Council. All Council Members
noted that the process would eventually lead to a district-based election in 2020 since
the City did not have a legally defensible choice to stay with at-large elections.

At the third public hearing held on February 20,2019, the City Council was presented
with multiple draft maps submitted by the community and vetted by NDC. When the
agenda item was called by the Mayor, the City Attorney provided a brief overview of the
CVRA and the City Council's next steps. He noted that the CVRA forces cities to move
to district elections; that there was no winning on this issue; and that the City would be
"extremely likely to lose any litigation." Mr. McEntire presented on behalf of NDC. Part of
his comments noted that so long as a district map met the legal requirements of federal
and state law, all other considerations regarding a map were policy decisions made by
the City Council. All Council Members noted that the City did not have any choice
regarding going toward district-based elections, particularly since the City received a
letter threatening litigation from SVREP's attorney. Council Member Real Sebastian
stated that this was an item that she brought to the City Council's attention because a
number of cities, including the City of South Pasadena, received similar letters. She
further explained that moving to district-based elections was a financially prudent action
and that district-based elections may encourage excellent candidates to run for City
Council.

On March 20,2019, the City Council held its fourth public hearing to consider district
maps. While responding to a hypothetical question posed by Council Member lng, Mr.
McEntire specifically stated that the City Council had to put districts into an election
cycle. Council Member lng noted that the process was a little odd since the City would
need to develop new maps in 2021 after receiving data from the 2020 census.

During the April 3, 2019 public hearing (the fifth), Mr. McEntire noted that this meeting
would be the first opportunity for the City Council to make policy decisions regarding the
various maps. ln response to queries from Council Member lng, both Mr. McEntire and
the City Attorney noted that the City Council would need to adopt the sequencing. Mr.
McEntire and the City Attorney reiterated that NDC provided suggestions for the

  Page 6 of 15

  Page 15 of 214
 sequencing and that sequencing would determine the seats up for election in 2020.
lndeed, the City Attorney specifically stated that "legally you can put the sequencing in
any order you want." The City Attorney further noted that there was no legal
requirement that the City Council accept the maps that were provided by the public or at
all. lndeed, the City Council could direct that a different map be drafted or variations of

 A refresher regarding the CVRA may be helpfulwhen discussing the items listed above.
Understanding the CVRA first requires an overview of the Federal Voting Rights Act
("FVRA';.s Federal law prohibits state and local governments from imposing voting laws
that result in discrimination against minority groups. This is partially accomplished by
prohibiting "minority vote dilution," i.e., instances where minority voters as a group,
although not prevented from voting, are unable to elect their preferred candidates
because they are usually outvoted by the majority. To prevent such dilution, the FVRA
prohibits public agencies from redistricting or using election methods that interfere with
a protected minority group's ability to elect candidates of its choice on an equal basis
with other voters. Under the FVRA, a plaintiff is not required to show intentional
discrimination by governmental officials in order to establish a violation. Rather, a
plaintiff must prove that minority vote dilution may be remedied by switching to a district-
based election system.

FVRA cases were largely effective in Southern states (where voting was persistently
polarized). ln California, however, voting is less polarized, the electorate is more
diverse, and minority groups are less geographically concentrated. These
circumstances often make it impracticalto create a majority-minority district as required
under the FVRA. Because of this, the California Legislature enacted the CVRA.

Generally, the CVRA has broader applicability than the FVRA. The CVRA prohibits both
at-large elections that prevent minority members from electing their chosen candidates
and also elections that impair the ability of minority voters to influence elections. A
plaintiff may establish liability simply by proving the existence of "racially polarized
voting."6

Racially polarized voting exists when two racial groups vote differently from each other,
i.e., the electoral choices preferred by voters in a protected class (a minority group) are
different from those of the rest of the electorate (the majority). At-large elections may
not be imposed or applied in a manner that impairs the ability of a protected class to
elect candidates of its choice or its ability to influence the outcome of an election.T

lf a court finds a violation of the CVRA, it must implement "appropriate" remedies that
are tailored to remedy the violation. These include imposing district-based elections or
enjoining the certification of the election results.s Additionally, the CVRA requires the
court to award attorneys' fees and costs to a prevailing plaintiff.e

The CVRA is a legislative gift to plaintiff attorneys. ln fact, plaintiff lawyers drafted it. lf
the California Legislature truly believed there is some inherent inequity in at-large
election systems, it could have simply mandated district-based election systems for
public agencies statewide. lnstead, the California Legislature designed a law that will
ultimately lead to the same end while guaranteeing a windfall to plaintiff attorneys - and
corresponding damage to already-strained local budgets - along the way.

The drafters of the CVRA did their best to ensure that mounting a defense is essentially
futile. There is no need for a plaintiff to demonstrate that the problem of racially
polarized voting is capable of being remedied. The mere existence of racially polarized
voting on any scale is enough to establish liability and force a local agency to abandon
at-large elections and move to a district-based electoral system.

ensures that plaintiffs have nothing to lose and much to gain, regardless of whether the

TO:  The Honorable Mayor and City Council
FROM:  Jim Smith, Chief of Police
SUBJECT:  Authorize Purchase of Ford Ranger XL 2WD SuperCab Utility Truck
  and Emergency Equipment

RECOMMENDATION:
It is recommended that the City Council:
  1. Waive bidding requirements pursuant to Monterey Park Municipal Code Section
  3.20.050(5) and authorize the City Manager or designee to execute a contract
  with Wondries Fleet Group, in a form approved by the City Attorney, for the
  purchase of one, 2O2O Ford Ranger XL 2WD SuperCab Utility Truck through
  Wondries Fleet Group;
  2. Authorize the City Manager or designee to execute a contract in a form approved
  by the City Attorney for the conversion/up-fitting of one 2020 Ford Ranger XL
  2WD SuperCab Utility Truck through West Coast Lights and Siren;
  3. Authorize the City Manager or designee to execute a contract with Bearcom /
  Motorola Solutions, in a form approved by the City Attorney, for the purchase of
  one Motorola APX 8500 All Band Police Radio for the 2020 Ford Ranger XL
  2WD SuperCab Utility Truck through Bearcom / Motorola Solutions;
  4. Take such additional, related, action that may be desirable.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:
The 2019-20 budget includes $50,000.00 for the replacement and conversion/up-fitting
of one parking enforcement vehicle for the Traffic Bureau of the Police Department.
Staff researched optional vehicles and determined the 2020 Ford Ranger XL 2WD
SuperCab Utility Truck is the best replacement choice as this vehicle meets the Police
Department's needs. As such, Staff recommends the purchase of one 2020 Ford
Ranger XL 2WD SuperCab Utility Truck with appropriate emergency equipment.

BACKGROUND:
The Police Department's Traffic Bureau has three units that are Ford Ranger Utility
trucks with the first one being put into service in 2008, which is still in service. These
units have a proven track record of reliability. The 2020 Ford Ranger XL 2WD
SuperCab Utility Truck comes standard with a 2.3 Eco-Boost engine, Electronic 10-
speed select shift automatic transmission, 2 wheel drive, air bags, as well as an anti-
lock braking system. The 2020 Ford Ranger XL 2WD SuperCab Utility Truck's comes
with a 5-year/60,000 mile power train warranty (major engine and transmission
components) and a 3-yearl36,000 mile bumper to bumper warranty.

This vehicle is available through a joint purchase program generally for larger agencies
such as the State of California (C.H.P.) and Los Angeles County (Sheriffs). Under joint
purchase, participating agencies can acquire goods and services at the lowest price
possible through volume discount without repeating the bid process. Joint Purchase is
a permitted purchasing method per Monterey Park Municipal Code Section 3.20.050(5).

Sourcewell (NJPA), a Special District of Government and Cooperative Purchasing

RECOMMENDATION:

It is recommended that the City Council:
  1  . Waive further reading, and introduce an ordinance Title 16 and 17 of the
  Monterey Park Municipal Code for adoption;
  2. Scheduling a public hearing on November 20, 2019 for the second reading and
  adoption of the Ordinance; and/or

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY:

The 2019 California Building Standards Code takes effect on January 1, 2020 ("CBSC').
These are part of the uniform codes imposed by the California Legislature every three
years via Title 24 of the California Code of Regulations. Health and Safety Code 517958
allows local governments to amend the CBSC based upon local climatic, topographical,
and geological conditions, or for administrative reasons.

The Public Works and Fire Departments are proposing amendments to the Monterey
Park Municipal Code relating to building code regulations for the purpose of complying
with State requirements and to update current administrative and technical standards.
The last code adoption with amendments to the Monterey Park Municipal Code relating
to building code regulations was November 16, 2016.

This ordinance would amend portions of the proposed 2019 CBSC and adopt the 2019
Edition of the CBSC.

TYPE OF ACTION (LEGISLATIVE)

The recommended action includes amending Titles 16 and 17 of the Monterey Park
Municipal Code byadopting the 2019 Edition of the CBSC. ln considering such action,

the City Council acts in its discretionary legislative capacity (formulating rules that apply
to all future cases). For the proposed amendments, the City Council must find that they
are reasonably necessary because of local climatic, geological or topographical
conditions (Health and Safety Code S 17958.7). These findings, and the facts upon
which they rely, are included within the draft Ordinance.

BACKGROUND:

The California Building Standards Commission is authorized by the California Building
Standards Law (Health and Safety Code SS 18901 through 18949.31 ) to administer the
processes related to the adoption, approval, publication, and implementation of
California's building codes.

California Code of Regulations ("CCR"), Title 24, also known as the CBSC, is a
compilation of three types of building criteria from three origins:
  . Building standards that have been adopted by state agencies with change from
  building standards contained in national model codes;
  e Building standards that have been adopted and adapted from the national model
  code standards to meet California conditions; and
  o Building standards, authorized by the California legislature, that constitute
  extensive additions not covered by the model codes that have been adopted to
  address particular California concerns.

Since 1989, the Commission has published triennial editions of Title 24 in lheir entirety.
These building codes are comprised of 12 parts containing the regulations that govern
and serve as the basis for the design and construction of all buildings and structures in
California.

California law requires that the City Council conduct a public hearing before second
reading of ordinances that adopt the CBSC by reference. Staff recommends that the
City Council set a Public Hearing for the second reading of the Ordinance at its
November 20, 2019 meeting.

FISCAL IMPACT:

The recommended actions will result in no financial impact to the City's General Fund.
The cost to administer this process is captured through various building, fire, and
engineering permits and fees.

CEQA:

(California Public Resources Code SS 21000, et seq., "CEQA") and the regulations
promulgated thereunder (14 California Code of Regulations $$ 15000, et seq., the
"CEQA Guidelines") because it consists only of minor revisions and clariflcations to an

inspections and the Building Official has authority to accept reports of inspection by
approved agencies or individuals. Reports of such inspections must be in writing and be
certified by a responsible officer of such approved agency or by the responsible individual.

to report upon unusual technical issues that arise, subject to the approval of the
appointing authority.

l04.s ldentification. The Building Official and appointees must carry proper identification
when inspecting structures or premises in the performance of duties under the codes.

109.1 Grounds for Appeal. Any aggrieved party may appeal any of the following
decisions of the Fire Chief:
  1. Disapproval of any application.
  2. Refusal to grant any permit applied for when it is claimed that the provisions of this
  California Fire Code do not apply.
  3. lnterpretation of this California Fire Code.

  materials to types of construction or methods.

109.2 Written Decision. Any such decision must be in writing and a copy thereof will be
served upon the applicant, if any, by mail. Any such decision will be final, unless an appeal
will be filed there from, within the time and in the manner prescribed by this section.

109.3 Appeal Procedure. Any person dissatisfied with any such determination or
decision of the Fire Chief has the right of appeal via the Administrative Civil Review
Process established under the provisions of Chapter 5.48 of the Monterey Park Municipal
Code.

109,4 Notice of Appeal. Any person desiring to take such an appeal must, within five
days after receipt of the written decision of the Fire Chief, file a written notice of appeal
with the Fire Chief for further review through an Administrative Hearing. Such written
notice of appeal must be on a form provided by the Monterey Park Fire Department and
contain such information as may be required for the Administrative Review.

109.5 Hearing. Each such appeal will be set for hearing for the Administrative Review.
Not less than five days before the date of such hearing, written notice of the time and

The City Council finds as follows

SECTION 1: Pursuant to the requirements of Health and Safety Code 517958.7, the City
Council finds that there are local climatic, geographic, and topographic con ditions
justifying the various local amendments to the California Building Standards Code as set
forth herein.

SECTION2: S pecifically, the City Council finds

  A.  Climatic Conditions

  1  The City of Monterey Park is a densely populated area within a
  climate system capable of producing major winds, fire and rain
  related disasters, including but not limited to those caused by the
  Santa Ana winds and El Niflo (or La Nifra) subtropical-like weather.
  This region is especially susceptible to more active termite and wood
  attacking insects and microorganisms.

  2  Hot, dry Santa Ana winds are common to all areas within the City of
  Monterey Park. These winds, which can cause small fires which
  spread quickly, are a contributing factor to the high fire danger in the
  area, and create the need for an increased level of fire protection'
  This added protection will supplement normal fire department
  response available and provide immediate protection for life and
  safety of multiple occupancy occupants during fire occurrences.

  3  Los Angeles County and the City of Monterey Park are located in a
  semi-arid Mediterranean type climate which predisposes all fuels,
  including wood shingles to rapid ignition and spread of fire'
  Therefore, there exists  a
  need for additional fire protection
  measures.

  4  The warm, dry climate is conducive to swimming pools which creates
  a higher probability of child drowning where pools are unprotected.

  B  Geological Conditions

  1.  The City of Monterey Park is a densely populated area having
  buildings and structures constructed over and near a vast array of
  fault systems capable of producing major earthquakes, including but
  not limited to the 1994 Northridge Earthquake, the 1987 Whittier
  Narrows Earthquake, the 1971 San Fernando Earthquake and the

  Page 97 of 120
  Page 189 of 214
   1933 Long Beach Earthquake.

2  The October 17,1989, Santa Cruz earthquake resulted in only one
  major San Francisco fire in the Marina district. But, when combined
  with the 34 other fires and over 500 responses, the department was
  taxed to its full capabilities. The Marina fire was difficult to contain
  because mains supplying water to the district burst during the
  earthquake. lf more fires had been ignited by the earthquake, it would
  have been difficult for the fire department to contain them. This
  situation creates the need for both additional fire protection
  measures and automatic on-site fire protection for building
  occupants since a multitude of fires may result from breakage of gas
  and electric lines as a result of an earthquake. As noted by "Planning
  Scenario on a Major Earthquake Department on of the Newport-
  lnglewood Fault Zone, 1988, State Conservation," "unfortunately
  meeting the minimum earthquake standards of building codes barely
  places a building on the verge of being legally unsafe."

3  Traffic and circulation congestion presently existing in the City of
  Monterey Park often challenges fire department response times.
  This condition will be exacerbated by any major disaster, including
  any earthquake wherein damage to the highway system will occur.
  This condition makes the need for additional on-site protection for
  p roperty occupants necessary.

4  Placement of multiple occupancy buildings, location of arterial roads,
  and fire department staffing constraints due to recent revenue-
  limiting state legislation have made it difficult for the fire department
  to locate additional fire stations and provide manpower sufficient to
  concentrate fire companies and personnel to control fires in high
  density apartment or condominium buildings. Fire Department
  equipment does not allow easy access to areas of buildings greater
  than 55 feet above the level of Fire Department vehicle access.
  These conditions create the need for built-in onsite fire protection
  systems to protect occupants and property until firefighting
  apparatus and personnel arrive on the scene.

5  The City of Monterey Park is located in an area subject to a climatic
  condition of high winds and low humidity. This combination of events
  creates an environment which is conducive to rapidly spreading fires.
  Control of such fires requires rapid response. Obstacles generated
  by a strong wind, such as fallen trees, street lights and utility poles,
  and the requirement to climb 75 feet vertically up flights of stairs will
  greatly impact the response time to reach an incident scene.
  Additionally, ASCE-7, Section 6, Figure 6 - 2 Height Adjustment
  Table identifies a significant increase in the amount of wind force at
  60 feet above the ground. Use of aerial type firefighting apparatus
  above this height would place rescue personnel at increased risk of
  injury.
  Page 98 of 120
  Page 190 of 214
   6  The City of Monterey Park is located in the middle of a seismically
  active area. The viability of the public water system would be
  questionable at best after a major seismic event. This would leave
  tall buildings vulnerable to uncontrolled fires due to a lack of available
  water and an inability to pump sufficient quantities of any available

2A. RESOLUTION DECLARING THE MONTH OF NOVEMBER AS ''MOVEMBER''
  TO RAISE AWARENESS TO PROSTATE AND OTHER MALE CANCERS

  The Movember Foundation is the leading global organization committed to
  changing the face of men's health. The Movember community has raised $800
  million to date and funded over 1,200 programs in 21 countries. This is saving and
  improving the lives of men affected by prostate cancer, testicular cancer and
  mental health problems.

  The Foundation challenges men to grow moustaches during Movember (formerly
  known as November), to spark conversation and raise vital funds for its men's
  health programs. To date, over 5 million moustaches have been grown worldwide.

  The mustaches are a symbol to promote awareness regarding men's health issues
  and encourage yearly checkups regarding prostate and testicular cancer. The
  groMh of a new moustache prompts a conversation, which in turn generates
  awareness and educates people on the health issues men face.

  The Vision of the Movember Foundation is to have an everlasting impact on the
  face of men's health.

2ts. MARCH 3,2020 ELECTION MATTERS
  "Preserving the integrity of the electoral process, preventing corruption, and
  sustaining the active, alert responsibility of the individual citizen in a democracy for
  the wise conduct of government are interests of the highest importance." The
  current sitting City Council engaged in a 15-month process (including seven public
  hearings, several noticed meetings, and numerous discussions) which concluded
  in May 2019 with the Council deciding to switch from an at-large to a district- based
  Council Member election process in compliance with the California Voting Rights
  Act ("CVRA"). This was intended to avoid a likely successful and very expensive
  legal challenge to the City's at-large election process. Switching back to an at-large
  election, even if it is just for one election cycle, just days before the nomination
  period opens for candidates to begin qualifying to run for City Council is extremely
  risky from a legal perspective and very likely indefensible. ln fact, it could result in
  a court imposing its own district-based process upon the City either before or after
  the March 2020 election, and the potential invalidation of the March election results
  if the Council switches back to an at-large process.

  More specifically, as to ltem No. 2(a) (of City Council recommendation), it does not
  appear that findings can be made to support adoption of an urgency ordinance.
  The City's administrative record developed over 15-months for transitioning from
  at-large to district elections clearly shows that changing back to at-large elections
  would expose the City to significant liability under the CVRA and Civil Rights law. lt
  does not appear that there is any legitimate basis to defend against a potential
  challenge to such an urgency ordinance. lf it loses a legal challenge, the City
  would pay not only for its own defense costs but also those of the prevailing party.
  Taking the action in ltem No. 2(a) is contrary to existing law and to the main reason
  that the entire City Council commenced implementing (and the majority of the City
  Council approved) the district election process.
   67 -226
  November 6,2019
  The same legal issues also arise regarding ltem No. 2(b) (of City Council
  recommendation): if the City Council repealed district elections pursuant to ltem
 No. 2(a), the City could be immediately sued by persons asserting that such action
 constitutes CVRA and Civil Rights violations. This is true even though on October
 16th the Council majority discussed the potential that the City would return to
 district-based elections in the future and give voters the chance to decide the
 sequence of district elections. Because three City Council seats are up for election
 in March 2020, the current Council cannot commit the next City Council to take
 such an action. ln addition to the legal risks identified above (as explained below in
 detail), if the City reverts back to at-large voting it must restart the process for
 switching back to district-based voting (which requires at least four public
 hearings). There is insufficient time to complete this process for the March 2020
 election as the cutoff date for placing matters on the ballot is December 6, 2019.
 Finally, there are 10 different potential combinations for sequencing the district
 elections. This would require 10 different ballot questions to determine which
 option the electorate prefers (the ballot measure receiving the most votes would
 prevail). A cost estimate for these 10 ballot propositions is approximately $230,000
 (County fees to place on ballot), plus staff and legal costs.

 Accordingly, it is strongly recommended that the Council only take the action in
 Item No. 1 (of City Council recommendation).

  The 2019 California Building Standards Code takes effect on January 1,2020
  ("CBSC'). These are part of the uniform codes imposed by the California
  Legislature every three years via Title 24 of the California Code of Regulations.
  Health and Safety Code S17958 allows local governments to amend the CBSC
  based upon local climatic, topographical, and geological conditions, or for
  administrative reasons.

  The Public Works and Fire Departments are proposing amendments to the
  Monterey Park Municipal Code relating to building code regulations for the purpose
  of complying with State requirements and to update current administrative and
  technical standards. The last code adoption with amendments to the Monterey
  Park Municipal Code relating to building code regulations was November 16,2016.

  This ordinance would amend portions fo the proposed 2019 CBSC and adopt the
  2019 Edition of the CBSC.
